strengths: SGDRO addresses a relevant computer vision problem: maintaining minority-group performance under distribution shift. Combining an overall-loss SAM perturbation with group-DRO updates is simple, architecture-independent, and described with usable pseudocode.

Waterbirds provides a controlled comparison against GDRO with the same regularization. Across five seeds, SGDRO improves both minority-group accuracies: LW from 86.5% to 87.2% and WL from 88.1% to 89.3%. Group-average accuracy increases from 90.4% to 90.6% (Table 1).

The curvature measurements support the empirical motivation. Under the same regularization, SGDRO has smaller largest and second-largest Hessian eigenvalues than GDRO for every Waterbirds group; the overall largest eigenvalue decreases from 356.6 to 268.7 (Table 2).

Evaluation extends to six DomainBed datasets with three repeated runs. SGDRO achieves 71.4% average accuracy versus 70.1% for GDRO and 70.9% for ERM, indicating useful improvements beyond Waterbirds (Table 3).
weaknesses: The central guarantees are unsupported. Section 3.1 offers a local Taylor interpretation, without establishing convergence, common flat minima, or worst-group generalization. Its expansion also incorrectly uses the overall-loss gradient and Hessian where the active group's gradient and Hessian are required. Correcting these symbols would still leave the substantive gap: a perturbation maximizing overall loss need not expose directions of high sensitivity for an individual group.

The relationship between the objective and update is insufficiently justified. Equation 4 makes the perturbation depend on the parameters, while Algorithm 1 treats it as fixed during differentiation. Because this perturbation is selected using a different loss from the outer group objective, the usual exact-inner-maximization justification for SAM does not directly apply. The resulting update is a plausible heuristic, but its approximation to the stated objective is not analyzed.

The claimed alleviation of the average-versus-worst-group trade-off is not demonstrated. In Table 1, the 0.7-point worst-group improvement over GDRO accompanies a 0.7-point decline in average accuracy, from 93.8% to 93.1%; both majority groups also deteriorate. These results establish a different operating point, without establishing an improved trade-off. The worst-group gain is also modest relative to the reported variability, whose interpretation as standard deviation or standard error is unspecified for Waterbirds.

The distinctive design choices are not isolated experimentally. There is no comparison against SAM applied directly to the group-DRO loss, no ablation comparing overall-loss and group-loss perturbations, and no ablation of updating group weights using perturbed losses. DomainBed omits SAM altogether. Consequently, the results do not establish whether the proposed coupling contributes beyond the benefits of its existing components. This is particularly consequential for a contribution built from two established optimization methods.

Reproducibility is only partial. Although pseudocode, seed counts, and references to baseline settings are provided, the manuscript does not explicitly specify the experimental backbones, minibatch handling of groups, or the DomainBed perturbation-radius search space. Smaller presentation issues include the tautological Equation 2 and the unfinished sentence in Section 3.2; these are readily correctable and do not determine the recommendation.

The balance favors Weak Reject: the empirical gains and consistent curvature reductions are worthwhile, but the unsupported central guarantees and insufficient validation of the specific algorithmic choices outweigh the currently established contribution.
